passage: The kabaddi selection was at the district ground in Karnal, and Simran, fifteen, stood by the bus stand with her stomach churning. 'I can't do this,' she told her teammate Zubin. 'I feel sick. I'm too scared. Let's just go home.' Zubin frowned. 'You've been talking about this selection for a month.' Simran sat on the low wall. Her Nani's words came back: stop, and notice all of it. So she did. Stomach churning. Hands tingling, but not cold. A grin she couldn't stop when she thought of the ground. And a hollow feeling: she'd been too nervous to eat breakfast. 'I think,' she said slowly, 'I'm hungry and excited. Not only scared.' She ate the roti in her bag. The churning eased. When the bus came, she got on.

qa.a: At the district ground in Karnal.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling by the bus stand at first?
qa.a: She felt sick and scared, wanting to go home.

passage: At Warsaw airport, Olga, sixteen, waited for Fatima, her pen-pal from Morocco, whom she'd written to for two years but never met. Her stomach was churning so hard she thought she might be ill. What if Fatima didn't like her? What if this was a terrible idea? She almost texted her mother to take her home. Then she made herself stop by the window and check. Heart fast. Cheeks warm. A silly smile each time the arrival board changed. And she'd had nothing but a coffee since morning. This wasn't dread. It was excitement, and hunger, all mixed up. She bought a pastry and ate it slowly. When Fatima came through the gate, waving wildly, Olga's stomach flipped again, and this time she knew exactly what it meant. She ran to hug her.

passage:
Ward note, evening shift
I've been watching Swati, our charge nurse, do something simple before every handover. She stands in the corridor, closes her eyes for about a minute and checks herself: jaw, shoulders, stomach, breath. Today I asked her about it. She said, 'If my jaw's clenched, I'm stressed. If my stomach's hollow, I'm hungry. If my breath's short, I need a minute before I talk to anyone.' Today she noticed she was hungry and tense, so she ate a banana and rolled her shoulders before handover. It went smoothly, and she stayed patient when a relative got angry. Last month, before she started this, she snapped at a junior. I'm going to suggest the whole team try it.
Farhan, ward manager

qa.a: About a minute.

qa.q: What did Swati feel before today's handover?
qa.a: She felt hungry and tense, which her body check revealed.

qa.q: What does the body scan help Swati avoid?
qa.a: Snapping at others, by catching stress or hunger early and dealing with it first.

qa.q: How might the relative have experienced Swati's patience?
qa.a: The relative probably felt heard and calmer because Swati did not react sharply.

grounding: Shows a person pausing for a quick body scan of jaw, shoulders, stomach and breath, which catches stress and hunger before they become snapping.

Campus doctor's note, Tuesday
Gargi, twenty, came to the health centre convinced something was wrong with her heart. She described a racing heartbeat at night, a clenched jaw so sore she couldn't chew, a stiff neck and an upset stomach, all during placement season. She was frightened. I listened carefully and checked her thoroughly. Her heart and other checks were normal. I explained that stress can show up in the body as a racing heart and tension, and that her symptoms were real, not imagined. She visibly relaxed when she understood this. We talked about sleep, meals and slow breathing, and I referred her to the counsellor. I asked her to come back if anything changes.
Madhav

Saturday
Placements are killing me. For two weeks my heart has been racing at night, thudding so hard I can hear it in the pillow. My jaw aches from clenching and my stomach is a mess. I was sure I had a heart problem. Today I finally went to the doctor. Dr Francis listened properly, did an ECG, and everything was normal. Then he said, 'Your heart is healthy. What you're feeling is stress, and stress is very physical.' I almost cried with relief. The symptoms are still there, but knowing what they are makes them less scary. He suggested slow breathing before bed, fewer late coffees and walks. Tonight my heart raced for a bit, and instead of panicking, I breathed.
Uma

Dear Ramesh,
I'm writing because I don't think I can say this properly in a meeting.
For the past eight months, I've been doing two people's jobs since Arjun left. I've had four colds this year. My back aches all the time, and I'm tired even after a full night's sleep. Worst, I've stopped caring about work I used to love. I sit at my desk and feel nothing.
I took a week's holiday in March, thinking it would fix this. It didn't. Two days back and I felt exactly the same.
I think my body is telling me the workload needs to change, not just that I need a break. Could we talk about hiring for Arjun's role or moving some projects? I want to keep doing good work here.
Sharmila

passage: In the staff room of the school where he taught, Lalit, twenty-five, pressed a hand to his stomach again. It was the third upset this month, plus headaches every evening and poor sleep. Dear Binita,
You were right, and I'm writing to tell you so.
When you visited, you noticed my eye twitching, my jaw clenched and that I was getting headaches every afternoon. I brushed it off. But it got louder: my stomach started playing up too, and I was waking at four every morning.

Love,
Damini
